summary: Initial dedicated capacity discovery for Aperture Health. Main focuses: strict tenant isolation needs (HIPAA-adjacent workloads), burst handling for unpredictable nightly inference spikes, and scaling/rollback playbooks. Customer leaning toward Dedicated but evaluating private VPC for data residency and stronger control. Action: pricing + benchmark plan and a technical deep-dive to run a small load test.
topics: tenant isolation and multi-tenant tenancy patterns
transcript:
[00:00] Tom Kruger: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call — Tom from Redwood, Maya the SE.
[00:09] Liam Park: Hey, Liam here. Sara and Raj on my side too.
[00:13] Sara Gomez: Hi all.
[00:15] Tom Kruger: Great. High level goal for today's call is to understand your capacity needs and isolation constraints so we can size a Dedicated pool and propose a burst strategy that meets your compliance needs. Does that sound right?
[00:28] Raj Menon: Yep, that's right. We run patient-facing NLP features — PHI-like content — so isolation and auditability are big. We also see big bursts around midnight when our nightly jobs and user analytics overlap.
[00:42] Maya Chen: Cool. Can you give us an idea of current traffic shape — baseline QPS and those spike characteristics?
[00:49] Liam Park: Baseline chat QPS is around 12 qps, peaks up to 220 qps for 3-7 minutes, once or twice a day. Also, batch scoring jobs start at 23:30 for about 30-90 minutes which cause sustained high token rates.
[01:09] Maya Chen: That's helpful. Do you have SLOs or p95 latency goals?
[01:13] Liam Park: We're targeting p95 < 300ms for simple prompts, < 800ms for longer context requests. Cost is a concern but availability and compliance beat price.
[01:24] Tom Kruger: Understood. A few clarifying Qs: Are you looking for Dedicated with strict single-tenant nodes, or is isolation at the VM/container level sufficient?
[01:33] Sara Gomez: Prefer single-tenant GPU pools — we need guaranteed physical isolation for audits. At minimum we want tenant separation and no cross-tenant KV cache leakage.
[01:45] Maya Chen: Noted. On burst handling: we can do a steady reserved pool sized for baseline plus a burst buffer for short spikes. Burst can be supplied by pre-reserved spare GPUs or a soft-burst to hosted capacity with fallbacks — but soft-burst touches hosted infra, which may not meet your isolation constraints.
[02:06] Raj Menon: Right, soft-burst is problematic for us. Can you explain how Redwood's burst credit and reserved spillover works? We heard about "burst credits" but details matter.
[02:18] Tom Kruger: Sure. We offer two patterns: 1) Burst on Dedicated — we reserve a baseline and maintain a standby pool you pay a lower standby fee for, so you get cold spin-up within minutes. 2) Hybrid burst — on overflow we route to a compatible hosted model variant with stricter logging and data controls, but that still resides on our hosted plane. There is an option for private-burst into a customer-managed VPC if you're on Private plan but that requires additional setup.
[02:49] Liam Park: So private-burst into our VPC is possible? That might be ideal but sounds heavy.
[02:54] Maya Chen: It's possible. We call it Private Burst — effectively we pre-provision instances in your VPC that Redwood can route traffic to. It needs VPN and KMS integration, and we'd run a small bootstrap. It adds setup time and an ops agreement, but leaves data within your network.
[03:12] Sara Gomez: How long to spin up standby GPUs? If we take the standby approach, we need to ensure the handoff doesn't create cold-cache-induced latency spikes.
[03:22] Maya Chen: Spin-up is typically 90-180 seconds for a cold node, but we keep warm workers for critical paths. We also do prefix/KV cache warming before failover for known prompt sets. Some customers pre-warm with a small synthetic traffic stream.
[03:36] Liam Park: Hmm, synthetic warming is interesting. For PII/PHI we can't send real content. Does Redwood support cache warming with deterministic tokens or placeholders?
[03:45] Tom Kruger: Yes, we recommend using synthetic tokens that mirror length and token distribution but not real PHI. We'll share templates.
[03:53] Raj Menon: Security checklist: SOC2 Type II, encryption at rest with customer-managed KMS, SSO/SAML, RBAC, audit logs for token-level tracing — do you provide these out of the box on Dedicated/Private?
[04:06] Tom Kruger: SOC2 Type II yes. KMS integration is supported for Private and Dedicated via HSM-backed keys; for Hosted there are managed keys but customer-managed is offered on Private deployments. SSO/SAML and RBAC available in console; audit logs retent is configurable. We'll attach our security pack.
[04:25] Sara Gomez: And network isolation — VPC peering or private link support?
[04:30] Maya Chen: We support VPC peering, AWS PrivateLink, and on-prem VPN tunnels for Private. Dedicated can be deployed in a customer VPC for stricter network controls.
[04:39] Liam Park: Good. On pricing: how does standby cost compare to full reserved? Any ballpark numbers?
[04:46] Tom Kruger: Ballpark: standby is typically 15-25% of a full reserved GPU hourly commit, since you're paying for allocation but not full utilization. Full reserved is cheaper per-hour if you commit to more consistent usage. We can run a cost model once you share token/sec and average length.
[05:03] Sara Gomez: For billing granularity, do you bill by GPU-hour, token, or mixture? We need this for finance alignment.
[05:10] Tom Kruger: For Dedicated it's a mix: committed GPU capacity + per-token for usage above thresholds or for hosted fallback. We'll clarify exact terms in the proposal.
[05:19] Raj Menon: What about model variants? If we pick a specific quantized model for cost efficiency, can you fall back automatically to a higher-latency variant if that one fails?
[05:30] Maya Chen: Yes. We support model routing policies. You can pin a primary variant, and configure fallbacks in order of cost/latency. The routing policy is policy-as-config in the console. Sometimes model names in transcripts show as "Redwooed beta" — ignore that, that's the captions.
[05:45] Liam Park: Ha, I saw that before. Ok, we're also concerned about KV cache security — you mentioned earlier leakage. What prevents one tenant's KV cache from being read by another?
[05:56] Maya Chen: We namespace KV cache per-tenant with strict access controls. For single-tenant physical nodes there's no shared process space. In multi-tenant setups we do additional per-request tokenization and encryption at rest. There are occasional mislabels in automated transcripts — you'll see KV "cash" sometimes.
[06:12] Sara Gomez: Good to know. For the pilot, we'd likely want 4 GPUs reserved for baseline (to handle 12 qps), a standby of 2 GPUs, and a plan for private-burst into our VPC if possible. Is that a sensible starting point?
[06:24] Maya Chen: That sounds reasonable. We'll run a quick capacity calc: baseline needs depend on model choice and sequence lengths. If you share your representative prompt lengths and token rates we'll model it.
[06:35] Liam Park: We'll share a redacted prompt set and token length distribution.
[06:38] Tom Kruger: Perfect. Timeline wise, what's your pilot window?
[06:42] Raj Menon: We want pilot in August to validate nightly burst handling before Q4 rollout. So ideally setup and run benchmarks mid-July to July-end.
[06:52] Tom Kruger: We'll aim for that. Next — failure modes: what happens if standby fails to come up or private-burst has a routing issue?
[06:59] Maya Chen: We have an automated fallback policy: if Dedicated standby fails, traffic can be throttled or diverted to a protected hosted variant with controlled data handling, or we can fail-open to a lower-cost less-isolated path depending on your chosen policy. For you, given isolation needs, we'd prefer to fail-safely: queue requests and return a hotspot-guard message rather than spill into hosted.
[07:23] Liam Park: Queuing is acceptable for some endpoints but user-facing chat can't have long waits. We need graceful degradation — maybe degrade to shorter context responses first.
[07:33] Maya Chen: Exactly — degrade context length or reduce model size to maintain latency. We'll simulate those in the bench tests.
[07:41] Sara Gomez: On monitoring and tracing — can we get per-token latency traces and cost breakdowns per model/route in the console?
[07:49] Tom Kruger: Yes, Console provides token-level cost breakdown, per-route latency histograms, and request traces. Exportable to your observability stack (we support Datadog, Grafana).
[07:58] Raj Menon: Any pitfalls folks usually forget when doing Private-burst into customer VPCs?
[08:04] Maya Chen: Two big ones: firewall/NAT rules that block outbound health checks, and KMS key policies that don't allow Redwood's service principal to use the key. We'll provide a checklist. Also watch for strict egress inspection that mangles streaming websockets.
[08:20] Liam Park: Good call.
[08:22] Tom Kruger: Quick recap of agreed outcomes: Aperture will send token distribution + redacted prompt examples; Redwood will send pricing sheet with standby scenarios, security pack, and a benchmark plan. We'll schedule a tech-deep for mid-July to run a small load test. Any objections?
[08:38] Sara Gomez: No objections. One ask: include sample cache-warming templates that don't use PHI.
[08:44] Maya Chen: We'll include those in the benchmark repo.
[08:47] Raj Menon: And also an example SLA for failover behavior — queue vs spill — so we can sign off with compliance.
[08:55] Tom Kruger: Roger, will include failover SLAs in the proposal.
[08:58] Liam Park: Thanks, everyone.
[09:00] Tom Kruger: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifacts and calendar invite for the deep-dive.
[09:06] (call ends)
questions: How long to spin up standby GPUs and mitigate cold-cache latency?
Is private-burst into customer VPC possible and what are the ops requirements?
What are the guarantees and options for failing safely vs spilling to hosted?
notes: Customer prefers physical single-tenant nodes for audits
Synthetic cache-warming recommended for PHI avoidance
